content.title: How to Watch the Artemis II Launch in the First Crewed Moon Mission in More Than 50 Years
content.text: The United States is sending astronauts back to the moon for the first time in more than five decades — an exciting event that should make for some thrilling live TV.A crew of four astronauts is scheduled to lift off from NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida for the Artemis II mission, the first manned moon mission since Apollo 17 was carried out in December of 1972.It's been nearly 54 years since a mission like this has occurred — and excitement has reached a fever pitch.Here's how you can tune in to witness history.RELATED: Chicago Fire and P.D. Will Be Delayed Tonight on NBC: What to Know (DETAILS)The earliest that the Artemis II will lift off from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida is at 6:24 p.m. EDT on Wednesday, April 1, according to NASA. The agency, along with weather officers with the U.S. Space Force’s Space Launch Delta 45, will monitor the weather, with NASA stating that the forecast in the area for launch day shows an 80% chance of favorable weather conditions. There's a two-hour window for the launch, from 6:24 to 8:24 p.m. ET, according to TODAY. If the launch is postponed, there are two other windows for it to take place this week — on Thursday, April 2 (between 7:22 p.m. and 9:22 p.m. ET ) and on Friday, April 3 (between 8 p.m. and 10 p.m. ET.)Those looking to view the launch live should start tuning into ​​​​​NBC News NOW before 6:24 p.m. ET on Wednesday, April 1 to see what happens. NASA is also broadcasting the launch attempt live on its YouTube channel.What is NBC News NOW?Viewers have several options when it comes to catching the Artemis II launch on NBC News NOW, a 24/7 streaming network.The network can be accessed several ways, including by visiting NBCNews.com/now, or via the NBC News smartphone app, YouTube, or Peacock.Al Roker, the weather and feature anchor at TODAY, will be in Florida at the Kennedy Space Center to watch the launch live.RELATED: The Complete Cast of TODAY: Every Host and AnchorWhat to know about the Artemis II missionArtemis II will take two trips around Earth before orbiting the moon. The astronauts are set to return in 10 days, with the spacecraft landing in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of San Diego, California.The mission — rescheduled from an original February launch date — involves testing technologies that NASA will need for long-term lunar exploration and human missions to Mars, according to the agency.NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman (Artemis II commander), Victor Glover (Artemis II pilot), and Christina Koch (Artemis II mission specialist), along with Canadian Space Agency astronaut Jeremy Hansen (Artemis II mission specialist), make up the four-member Artemis II team."It’s a stepping stone to Mars, where we might have the most likelihood of finding evidence of past life," Koch said during a March news conference.
